LibraForge matching benchmark

2026-11-02 · LibraForge 22b5c9c · Audible public catalog (no login), US marketplace, Goodreads fallback

Want a test run again (a newer version of a tool, a different setting) or another tool added to the comparison? Open an issue to re-run a test or open an issue to add a tool. Every tool is scored the same way, on the same books and with the same metrics as below. Have audiobooks whose tags were never edited? Add them to the benchmark: it needs only each file's path, runtime and tags (one ffprobe command), never the audio.

Results · How each tool matches · Every book

4,044 audiobooks in their original state, before any matching: the tags LibraForge saved before it first wrote anything to a library's books, or another library's files as they were. Each book was matched again from those original tags, its folder path and its runtime, with no login, against the live catalog, the same way Metadata Forge matches a new book. Every book and every tool's result on it was then audited. Whether the tool picked the right book, another recording of it or the wrong book (and, when it held its pick, whether the held pick was right) was decided by hand, book by book. What the tool then left on the book was checked by script against each tool's own way of writing (below), so the same rule applies to every tool: a field is damaged when the book ends up with something wrong in it (written or kept from the file) or without something it is known to have (the narrator a listing of the book names, the series and number the file or folder gives). A tool that keeps the file's own details is judged on the book as it ends up. Each book's "reviewed by hand" line gives the hand note and what the checks found. A random 300 books were then audited a second time against the raw records: 37 of 2,100 verdicts (1.8%) were wrong, 26 from a check and 11 from a hand call; every kind of error found was corrected for all books. A fresh random 100 books, audited after that, had 3 wrong verdicts of 700 (0.4%), also corrected.

Percentages are of all books. Written: books the tool wrote, or for ReadMeABook identified. Correct of written: the books it wrote that ended up right. Right book of written also counts a book written with another recording's narrator or with one field off.

How each tool writes, and so what correct means for it

  • LibraForge, public catalog + Goodreads: Writes the listing's fields to the files. When the runtime or the narrator says the file is another recording, keeps the file's narrator, ASIN, year and ISBN. A series-only match writes the series alone.
  • AudioSilo: A confident match attaches the ASIN and fills only blank fields, so the file's title, narrator and series stay. Everything else waits in review.
  • Audiobookshelf Quick Match: Replaces the book's details with the listing's, in Audiobookshelf's database.
  • BookOrbit: Fetches the listing into its own records (title, authors, narrators, series), not into the files.
  • Grimmory: Fills or replaces each field from the provider's top result, field by field.
  • ReadMeABook: Picks a listing per book and writes nothing, to files or a library. Scored on whether the pick is the book.
  • beets (audible plugin): Writes the listing's fields to the files when it accepts the match; skips the rest.

What the audit found in LibraForge's writes

  • 60: No narrator: a Goodreads listing, or an Audible listing with none, left the narrator empty (often clearing the file's)
  • 30: A series written without its number, though the file or folder had it
  • 18: A decimal series number (3.5, 14.5) dropped
  • 18: A box set's range cut off the title ("Box Set (25-28)" written as "Box Set")
  • 13: The series left on the title ("9d6 (Caverns & Creatures)")
  • 13: Took the file's narrator field for another recording when it held the author, and kept the author as narrator
  • 12: Another recording's narrator written on a file that had no narrator tag
  • 9: A series number written with no series name ("#451" from "Fahrenheit 451")
  • 8: One number written on a multi-book set
  • 8: Took the file's narrator field for another recording when it held "Misc", and kept it
  • 6: No series written for a book in one
  • 5: A junk title kept ("01 Monster Core")
  • 4: A co-author missing
  • 3: Another title written (a Goodreads edition or a story in the collection)
  • 3: The series name written as the title
  • 2: The wrong series written in a series-only match
  • 2: A series made from the title (Goodreads)
  • 2: The wrong book written
  • 1: A junk series name ("Discworld, #27; Rincewind #7")

Compared with other tools

Each tool got the same original tags as files carrying them (silent files at the books' real folder paths; for tools that check runtime, as long as the real book) and was scored the same way. Only LibraForge and AudioSilo hold a match for review; the others apply what they accept.

Why AudioSilo matched 4,044 books in about a minute

Every other tool here asks a web service for each book: every search is a round trip to Audible or Goodreads, usually a second or so and often several per book, and most tools also pause between books so the service doesn't block them. Even spread over 5 workers, that adds up to about 29 minutes for LibraForge and hours for most of the others.

AudioSilo can skip all of that. AudioSilo is part of its own metadata project (audiosilo-meta, a community database released as CC0), and in mirror mode the server downloads the whole database once: one SQLite file of about 320,000 recordings of 300,000 works (a 517 MB download, about 2 GB on disk), with a full-text search index built in, refreshed daily from GitHub. Matching a book then is a query against that file on the same disk: no network, no rate limit, nothing to wait for. That came to about 15 milliseconds per book with its 2 workers, and not a single request to their service during the run, which is kind to their servers too.

The trade-off is coverage: it can only find what the community has added, which is why more of its books land in review or no match than LibraForge's. The speed is a design choice, not a shortcut: it searched every book and checked runtime on every match.

Setup per tool

  • AudioSilo (v2.5.1): "Match automatically" over the library, in mirror mode (a local copy of the community database, so the run made no calls to their service). Confident matches count as applied, "to review" as held.
  • Audiobookshelf Quick Match (v2.35.1, Audible US provider): the Quick Match button per book, which takes the first Audible result, looked up by the file's ASIN when it has one. Run one book at a time, as ABS's own Match All does.
  • BookOrbit: a library bulk metadata fetch with its default providers.
  • beets-audible (beets 2.14, the plugin's recommended settings): beet import -q, which applies strong matches and skips the rest; skipped books count as no match. beets was given each book's real runtime, since it scores candidates on track length.
  • LibraForge: lf_bench.py over the same files, public catalog with the Goodreads fallback on, 5 search workers.
  • Grimmory (v3.5.0): a library metadata refresh with Audible enabled and first for every field (Goodreads, then Google behind it), applied without review. Per provider it takes the top result: one keyword search, first result. It reads the iTunes-atom copies of the tags, which carry no ASIN.
  • ReadMeABook (v1.2.12): the Bulk Import scan, which picks an Audible match per book by itself (one catalog search on album, album artist and composer, first result). It groups folders by their tags, so books it merged into a parent folder count as no match. Its scan returns no series.
